description: Width tiers for Foundation Year Science — ACARA v9. Covers all 9 descriptors (U-strand, H-strand and I-strand). Foundation is a single year, not a band floor.
subject: Science

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor — the fewest contexts or task types that still genuinely satisfy the descriptor at Foundation level. Minimum is typically one context met with teacher guidance.
width_notes.typical_width: The full scope of the descriptor grounded in the most common elaboration cases. What a Foundation class that has engaged with the descriptor fully would have done.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding phenomena, cultural contexts or representation forms. First Nations directions included where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations treated as source data. Typical grounded in common cases; wider may infer within the descriptor's territory and year level.

AC9SFU01.minimum_width: Name at least two external features of a plant and two of an animal; sort a collection of living things into two groups and state the feature used.
AC9SFU01.typical_width: Use magnifying glasses or digital cameras to observe and name features of plants and animals; identify humans as animals and describe human features; sort collections of model animals using different feature-based grouping strategies; identify common features within familiar animal groups (fish, birds, reptiles).
wider: Observe fruits and vegetables and identify them as parts of plants — roots, flowers, fruits or leaves
Recognise First Nations Australians' use of observable features to group living things — examining cultural classification knowledge
Explore how First Nations Australians' observations of external features are replicated in traditional dance
elaborations: observing fruits and vegetables identifying them as roots, flowers, fruits or leaves
recognising humans as animals and describing human external features
using magnifying glasses or digital cameras to observe features of plants and animals
sorting model animal collections and explaining different grouping strategies
recognising First Nations Australians' use of observable features to group living things
exploring how First Nations Australians' observations are replicated in traditional dance

AC9SFU02.minimum_width: Describe at least three different ways objects can move with examples; compare two objects and describe how one factor (size, shape or material) affects their movement.
AC9SFU02.typical_width: Observe and describe movement types (roll, slide, bounce, spin); group toys by movement type; compare different-sized similar-shaped objects; explore how material affects ball movement; observe unusually shaped objects rolling; make predictions about movement then observe.
wider: Explore how the size and shape of traditional First Nations Australians' instructive toys influence their movement
Compare how different-sized similar-shaped objects (tennis, golf, marble, basketball) roll and bounce
Predict and observe how an unusually shaped object (egg, hexagonal block) moves down a slope
elaborations: observing how toys move and grouping by movement
observing and describing how unusually shaped objects move when rolled down a slope
comparing different-sized similar-shaped objects rolling and bouncing
exploring how material affects ball movement
exploring how size and shape of First Nations instructive toys influence movement

AC9SFU03.minimum_width: Identify the material of at least three objects; name one object made of more than one material; describe at least two observable properties of each of three materials.
AC9SFU03.typical_width: Observe and manipulate objects to identify materials; recognise multi-material objects; sort and group materials by properties (colour, hardness, texture, flexibility); create displays naming materials and exploring property vocabulary; use digital cameras on a materials scavenger hunt; suggest why object parts use different materials.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians make utensils for different purposes by combining different materials
Use a digital camera to collect images on a materials scavenger hunt
Suggest why different parts of everyday objects (saucepan, clothing) are made from different materials
elaborations: observing and manipulating objects to identify their materials
recognising that some objects are made of more than one material
sorting and grouping materials by observed properties
creating a display of materials and exploring property language
using a digital camera on a materials scavenger hunt
suggesting why different parts of objects use different materials
investigating how First Nations Australians combine materials to make utensils

AC9SFH01.minimum_width: Describe two ways people make observations; give one example of a question a scientist or person might ask about nature.
AC9SFH01.typical_width: Explore how scientists use senses and equipment to observe; view examples of observations (rock paintings, drawings, photos, reports); engage with scientist stories (Jane Goodall, Joseph Banks); notice how they observe and question; pose their own questions after viewing.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australians gain knowledge about land and resources through observation
Interact with stories or documentaries about scientists and notice observation and questioning methods
Watch a documentary and notice how scientists, engineers and citizen scientists ask questions — then pose own questions
elaborations: using senses and exploring how scientists use senses and equipment
viewing examples of observations including rock paintings, drawings, photos and reports
exploring how First Nations Australians gain knowledge through observation
interacting with stories about scientists like Jane Goodall or Joseph Banks
watching documentaries and noticing how scientists ask questions

AC9SFI01.minimum_width: Pose one question about an observed object or phenomenon; make one prediction and state what experience it is based on.
AC9SFI01.typical_width: Pose questions about everyday objects, materials and living things; make predictions before field work; make predictions about object movement; explain what experience grounds each prediction.
wider: Pose questions about plant parts: 'What part of a plant is broccoli?'
Make predictions about how an unusually shaped object might move down a slope
Make predictions about which plants and animals might be observed in the school grounds
elaborations: posing questions based on experiences about plant parts or object movement
posing questions about everyday objects and materials
making predictions before field work about plants and animals
making predictions about how unusually shaped objects might move

AC9SFI02.minimum_width: Follow at least two safety rules during an investigation; make observations using at least three senses; explain why taste is not used in science.
AC9SFI02.typical_width: Discuss and follow safety rules (sun safe, no running, no tasting, follow instructions); explain safety considerations for each sense; use magnifying glasses, binoculars and digital cameras to enhance observations; record observations in basic formats (numbers, dots, drawings, photos).
wider: Explain safety considerations for each sense used in investigations
Use magnifying glasses and digital cameras to observe plant and animal features in greater detail
Record observations using multiple formats — numbers, dots, drawings, voice recordings, digital photography
elaborations: discussing ways to conduct investigations safely
explaining safety considerations for touch, smell, sight and hearing
using provided tools to enhance observations of plants and animals
recording observations using numbers, dots, drawings, voice recordings, digital photography

AC9SFI03.minimum_width: Use a provided template to record or sort at least two observations; contribute to a class display; identify one simple pattern with guidance.
AC9SFI03.typical_width: Use provided tables and graphic organisers to sort images by features; collaborate on class displays; identify patterns of movement in objects; identify patterns in material uses; name a shared feature within a sorted group.
wider: Collaborate to create a display linking material samples to objects made from them
Identify patterns of movement in objects — balls roll, cars move on wheels
Identify patterns in uses of objects made of similar materials
elaborations: using provided tables and graphic organisers to sort plants and animals by features
collaborating to create displays linking materials to objects
identifying common features within familiar animal groups
identifying patterns of movement in objects with guidance
identifying patterns in uses of everyday objects made of similar materials

AC9SFI04.minimum_width: State whether a prediction matched an observation; describe at least one way the observation was the same as or different from the prediction.
AC9SFI04.typical_width: Revisit predictions and identify with guidance whether they matched; use a provided table to record prediction and observation side by side; compare field work observations with pre-field predictions; describe similarities and differences.
wider: Use a provided table to draw prediction and observation side by side and compare explicitly
Revisit predictions about field work observations and compare with what was actually found
Explore what to do when a prediction does not match — 'what can we do to find out more?'
elaborations: revisiting predictions and with guidance identifying whether they matched observations
comparing observations of plants or animals from field work with predictions
using a provided table to draw or dictate prediction and observation

AC9SFI05.minimum_width: Share one science observation or idea with others using at least one form beyond verbal (drawn, modelled, role-played or displayed).
AC9SFI05.typical_width: Share questions, predictions and observations through discussions and circle groups; recount nature experiences; show or describe object movement; role-play scientists using equipment; represent plant and animal features using materials; communicate using posters, collages, digital displays, drawings or storyboards.
wider: Acknowledge and explore First Nations Australians' ways of communicating information about anatomical features of plants and animals
Role-play how scientists use different equipment to make observations
Represent external features of plants and animals using blocks, modelling clay, craft materials or paper
elaborations: sharing questions, predictions and observations through discussions and circle groups
recounting experiences learning about nature at home or in conservation areas
acknowledging First Nations Australians' ways of communicating about plant and animal features
showing or describing how objects move in different ways
role-playing how people use equipment to make observations
representing plant and animal features using a range of materials
communicating using posters, collages, digital displays, drawings or storyboards
